Loral Corp. v. Moyes, 174 Cal. App. 3d 268 (1985) was the foundation for decades. It held employee non-solicitation provisions enforceable so long as they were reasonable in time and scope. This is the case most people are unknowingly relying on when they assume a 12-month non-solicit is fine.

Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, 44 Cal. 4th 937 (2008) undercut it. The California Supreme Court struck down a customer non-solicitation provision because it restricted Edwards from practicing as an accountant, and rejected the common-law rule-of-reason analysis, reasoning that the legislature could have written § 16600 to void only unreasonable restraints if that was the intent.  closed that question. The court disagreed with Loral and found employee non-solicitation agreements an unlawful restraint under § 16600 even though they don't entirely prevent employees from moving to a competitor — pointing out that the statute bans "restraints" on trade, not "prohibitions." Two federal decisions followed quickly: Barker v. Insight Global, LLC, 2019 WL 176260 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 11, 2019), and WeRide Corp. v. Kun Huang, 379 F. Supp. 3d 834, 852 (N.D. A disclaimer doesn't cure it, and Brown is the direct evidence — TGS tried exactly that structure and lost.

TGS had a sweeping definition plus two express exceptions. The court didn't stop at "there are carve-outs, so it's bounded." It examined whether the carve-outs had real content and found they didn't: the "generally known" exception was worthless in a field where profitability depends on methods not being generally known, and the prior-knowledge exception was conditioned on written records, which the court called absurd. The exceptions existed on paper and still failed.

Two features of California procedure make this worse than it looks. Under Dowell, once provisions are facially void the court does no further analysis — so your counterparty mounts a facial challenge and never has to develop a factual record about how the disclaimer would operate. And Edwards rejected the idea that a narrowly drawn restraint survives §16600, which forecloses the argument that your clause is reasonable in practice. A disclaimer is precisely the kind of provision that only does work in an as-applied inquiry the court won't reach.

**One clarification on what I actually drafted.** Section 2.1 does not require marking. It's disjunctive: information qualifies if it's designated confidential *or* if a reasonable person in the Receiving Party's position would understand it to be confidential given the content and circumstances. Unmarked information is covered. There's no tagging burden on you, and no gap if someone forgets to stamp a document.

**There's a real middle option** if you want the presumption to lean harder your way:

> 2.1 Definition. "Confidential Information" means non-public information relating to the Business that is disclosed by the Disclosing Party or its Representatives to the Receiving Party or its Representatives in connection with the Purpose. Information so disclosed is presumed to be Confidential Information. This presumption does not extend to general knowledge, skill, or experience in the [RELEVANT INDUSTRY] industry, or to information relating to that industry generally rather than to the Business, and the presumption is rebutted as to any information falling within Section 3.

That gets you a default of "everything counts," which is what you're after, while keeping two real boundaries: it's tied to your actual Business rather than your industry, and the exclusions in Section 3 are genuine because I already removed the written-records trap. The difference from TGS is that these limits have content — Brown's problem wasn't the presumption, it was that nothing meaningful survived the exceptions.

An NDA asserting that all information is confidential gives you nothing to point at. Some designation discipline, even informal, is what lets you show a court what you're protecting. The clause that claims the most often proves the least.
